level1.text: The refractive index of a soap film is $1.33$, and at one point its thickness is $420\,\text{nm}$. Light arrives at normal incidence on the film. What is the path difference between the waves reflected from the two surfaces of the film? Give your answer in nanometres.
The wavelength of red laser light in air is $633\,\text{nm}$. What is the wavelength of the light in magnesium fluoride, whose refractive index is $1.38$?

An $\text{MgF}_2$ coating ($n = 1.38$) is evaporated onto the glass of a camera lens so that light of wavelength $500\,\text{nm}$ is reflected as little as possible. The refractive index of the glass is $1.52$, and the light arrives at normal incidence. How thick is the thinnest such coating?

The refractive index of a soap film is $1.33$, and there is air on both sides of it. Light arrives at normal incidence on the film. How thick is the thinnest film that reflects light of wavelength $600\,\text{nm}$ most strongly?

The refractive index of the plastic of a spectacle lens is $1.60$. At normal incidence a single-layer anti-reflection coating would cancel the reflection completely if the waves reflected from its two surfaces were equally strong. What should the refractive index of the coating then be?
A soap film is in air, and light arrives at normal incidence on the film. At which surface does the reflected wave get inverted, that is, get a shift of half a wavelength, and why?
level1.answer: Only at the upper surface, because the light is reflected there from a material with a greater refractive index.

choices.text: At both surfaces, because there is exactly the same material, namely air, on both sides of the film.
choices.feedback: The material on both sides of the film is the same, but inversion depends on the refractive indices at the interface. Only a surface at which the refractive index increases inverts the wave, and the two surfaces are of different kinds.

choices.text: Only at the lower surface, because the light is reflected there from a material with a smaller refractive index.
choices.feedback: The other way round: from the film into air (1.33 → 1.00) the light is reflected from a material with a smaller refractive index, and then the wave is not inverted. The reflection at the lower surface keeps its phase.

choices.text: Only at the upper surface, because the light is reflected there from a material with a greater refractive index.
choices.feedback: Correct: from air into the film (1.00 → 1.33) the light is reflected from a material with a greater refractive index, and then the wave is inverted. That is why the reflection at the upper surface gets a shift of half a wavelength.

choices.text: At neither surface, because light arriving at normal incidence is reflected straight back.
choices.feedback: Normal incidence does not prevent inversion. A reflection always inverts the wave when the light arrives at an interface with a material of greater refractive index, regardless of the direction of incidence.

level1.text: On the surface of water ($n = 1.33$) there is an oil film whose refractive index is $1.47$. Light arrives from air at normal incidence on the film. How thick is the thinnest oil film that reflects light of wavelength $570\,\text{nm}$ most strongly?

A soap film ($n = 1.33$) is $300\,\text{nm}$ thick, and light arrives at normal incidence on the film. The wavelength of green laser light in air is $532\,\text{nm}$. How many wavelengths $\lambda$ fit into the path difference between the waves reflected from the two surfaces of the film?

level2.text: The thickness of a soap film ($n = 1.33$) is $240\,\text{nm}$ at one point, and there is air on both sides of it. White light arrives at normal incidence on the film. Which wavelength of visible light ($400$–$700\,\text{nm}$) is missing from the reflected light?

A glass lens ($n = 1.52$) has a $110\,\text{nm}$ thick $\text{MgF}_2$ coating ($n = 1.38$) on its surface. Light arrives at normal incidence on the coating. For which wavelength of visible light ($400$–$700\,\text{nm}$) is the reflection from the coating weakest?

An $\text{MgF}_2$ coating ($n = 1.38$) is made on glass ($n = 1.52$) so that it reflects light of wavelength $520\,\text{nm}$ as little as possible at normal incidence. The manufacturer wants a layer thicker than the thinnest possible. How thick is the second thinnest coating that reflects this wavelength most weakly?

In a beam splitter a thin titanium dioxide layer is made on glass ($n = 1.52$) so that it reflects light of wavelength $550\,\text{nm}$ as much as possible. Assume that the refractive index of the layer is $2.30$ and that the light arrives from air at normal incidence on the layer. How thick is the thinnest such layer?

The table gives example data: the thickness $d$ of a thin soap film and the wavelength $\lambda$ of visible light that is reflected most strongly, at five points. The film is in air, light arrives at normal incidence, and at all points the same order $k$ is reflected most strongly.

a) Draw a graph in which the wavelength $\lambda$ is a function of the thickness $d$, and fit a line to the points. Deduce the order $k$ and justify why the other possible order does not work.

b) Determine the refractive index $n$ of the film from the slope of the line.

The answer box takes the refractive index of part b).

data.caption: Wavelength reflected most strongly as a function of the thickness of a soap film (example data)

level2.text:
A student studied a soap film ($n = 1.33$) whose thickness is $250\,\text{nm}$ at one point and which has air on both sides. White light arrives at normal incidence on the film.

The student's solution: “The path difference is $2nd = 2 \cdot 1.33 \cdot 250\,\text{nm} = 665\,\text{nm}$. It is one whole wavelength of red light, so the waves of red light are in phase and reinforce each other. The film looks red at this point.”

a) What is the error in the student's reasoning?

b) Which wavelength of visible light ($400$–$700\,\text{nm}$) is really reflected most strongly at this point?

The answer box takes the wavelength of part b).

The table gives example data: the glass ($n = 1.52$) of a camera lens has an $\text{MgF}_2$ coating ($n = 1.38$), and the table gives the share $R$ of the light arriving at normal incidence that is reflected from the lens at different wavelengths.

The coating is the thinnest possible ($k = 0$), and it is designed to weaken the reflection as much as possible at one wavelength.

a) Draw a graph in which the reflected share $R$ is a function of the wavelength $\lambda$, and deduce from the table for which wavelength the coating is designed. How thick is the coating?

b) Using the shape of the graph, explain why the coated lens looks purple.

The answer box takes the thickness of the coating in part a).

data.caption: Reflection of a coated lens as a function of wavelength (example data)

level3.text: A soap film ($n = 1.33$) made in a vertical wire frame is lit with the yellow light of a sodium lamp, with wavelength $589\,\text{nm}$, arriving at normal incidence on the film. Gravity thins the film at the top, and the topmost part of the film looks black. Below it bright and dark horizontal bands alternate, and the film gets thicker downwards. How thick is the film at the second dark band, when the topmost black region is not counted as a band?

A camera objective has four separate glass lenses, that is, eight surfaces at which light passes from air into glass or from glass into air. Each surface is coated so that it reflects $1.3\,\%$ of the light arriving at it at normal incidence. Assume that the glass does not absorb light and that light reflected once no longer reaches the sensor. What percentage of the light entering the objective gets through it?

A soap film ($n = 1.33$) is in air, and white light arrives at normal incidence on the film. In the visible range the film reflects most strongly the wavelengths $630\,\text{nm}$ and $450\,\text{nm}$, and there are no other strongly reflected wavelengths between them. How thick is the film?

Oil has got onto the surface of water and forms a thin film. The refractive indices are $1.00$ for air, $1.47$ for oil and $1.33$ for water. White light arrives at normal incidence on the film. At one point the thickness of the film is $450\,\text{nm}$.

a) Deduce which of the surfaces inverts the reflected wave, and calculate which wavelengths of visible light ($400$–$700\,\text{nm}$) are reflected most strongly at this point. What colour is the point?

b) The film thins as the oil spreads. How thin has the film become when the wavelength reflected most strongly in part a) is reflected most weakly for the first time (destructive interference, $2nd = k\lambda$)?

c) Explain why the film looks dark and almost colourless at a point where its thickness is much smaller than the wavelength of visible light.

The answer box takes the thickness of part b).

Two identical glass plates ($n = 1.52$) are placed on top of each other so that they touch along one edge. A thin foil is placed between the plates at the other edge, and an air wedge ($n = 1.00$) is left between the plates.

The wedge is lit from above at normal incidence with the light of a sodium lamp, whose wavelength is $589\,\text{nm}$. Seen from above, evenly spaced dark fringes appear. Consider only the light reflected from the two surfaces of the air layer.

The table gives the distance $x$ of the dark fringes from the line of contact (example data). The fringe $k = 0$ is the line of contact. The foil is at a distance $L = 80\,\text{mm}$ from the line of contact.

a) Deduce which of the surfaces of the air layer inverts the reflected wave, and justify why the line of contact is dark.

b) Draw a graph in which the distance $x$ of the fringe is a function of the order (the ordinal number of the fringe) $k$, and fit a line to the points. Determine the fringe spacing $\Delta x$. By how much does the thickness of the air layer increase from one fringe to the next?

c) How thick is the foil? Give your answer in micrometres.

The answer box takes the thickness of part c).
